title: Learning Walks or Aimless Wanderings?
author: Samuel Crome
summary: Samuel Crome argues that the 'every lesson, every day' learning walk can be a powerful school-improvement lever, but only if leaders are purposeful about it. Too often it becomes a tokenistic routine, a cursory wander without remit or impact. He offers five questions for leadership teams to reflect on: whether the purpose is agreed and shared, what actually happens on a walk, what the walker needs to know beforehand, how observations are compared and fed back, and how staff are supported afterwards. He stresses that comparing notes across the team corrects the bias of small samples, such as seeing a new teacher only with a difficult class. Where a pattern of concern emerges, he recommends a coordinated plan involving the teacher, head of department and senior leaders that goes beyond observation to include planning support, debriefs and watching colleagues. Throughout, the tone should be supportive and non-judgemental.
points: Learning walks should begin with a purpose stated and shared by every member of the team, because leaders who set out with different agendas will miss things.
Leaders should agree in advance how long to stay in a room, how to respond to disruption and whether to speak to dysregulated pupils, then run scenarios so the whole team acts consistently.
Observations must be compared across the team, since one walker seeing a new teacher with a single class creates a biased small sample.

Where a teacher needs support, a coordinated plan should include the teacher, head of department and a senior leader, with planning help, debriefs and visits to colleagues rather than observation alone.
The learning walk is described as an expensive activity that only pays off when its data is shared, trends are spotted and next week's walks are made more purposeful.
quotes: But they should be a key driver of school improvement, because the amount of data you accrue across the team means you should be able to pinpoint what’s going well, and where more support is needed.

But learning walks don’t always add value. Often, they become a tokenistic routine, a cursory wander around the school, and something that just happens every day, without remit or purpose. And certainly without impact.
But we need to state our purpose at the start, so there is a shared understanding of what we are doing and why. If people are setting out with different agendas, then things will be missed.
Whatever you decide, there needs to be consistency across the team of learning walkers. This helps the children and staff know what to expect, and maintains your agreed upon culture.
Narrow sample size, but my opinion on Dave’s teaching hasn’t got off to a brilliant start.
So, that’s why we must compare. This is a team effort, and every lesson is different.
The success of a lesson depends both on the decisions the teacher makes in the lesson itself, but also fundamentally on the way they planned the lesson, too.
It’s an ongoing process that will both help them to improve but also to feel empowered.
